anchor: Let me not to the marriage
title: Let me not to the marriage of true minds
short: A definition of true love as constant; it echoes the marriage service, and Vendler reads it as a rebuttal of someone who claims love changes.
body: The sonnet is one of the most famous definitions of love in English and a favourite wedding reading, yet it belongs to the sequence addressed to a young man, and its 'marriage' is of minds, not a church wedding. Its opening echoes the Book of Common Prayer's marriage service, where the priest asks whether anyone knows of an 'impediment' to the union. Helen Vendler reads the poem as a reply in an argument, refuting an unspoken claim that love changes with circumstance (hence the emphatic 'O, no!'). The poem proceeds largely by negatives: it defines love by what it is not.

title: Admit impediments
short: To allow obstacles to a union; the word comes from the marriage service in the Book of Common Prayer (1559).
body: In the 1559 Book of Common Prayer the priest charges the couple that 'if either of you do know any impediment' why they may not lawfully marry, they should confess it, and the rubric provides for anyone who will 'allege and declare any impediment'. Shakespeare's speaker refuses to admit (acknowledge, allow) any such obstacle to the union of true minds. The enjambment ('true minds / Admit impediments') sets the key word at the start of a line, and the full stop in mid-line 2 gives the sentence a judicial firmness. Compare the attempts to stop the wedding in Much Ado About Nothing.

title: alters ... alteration; remover to remove
short: Love is not love if it changes when it finds change in the beloved, or bends to withdraw when the other withdraws.
body: Lines 3-4 use polyptoton, repeating a word in different forms: 'alters ... alteration', 'remover ... remove'. The figure enacts the false love it describes, which simply mirrors the other person's movements. 'Alteration' may mean a change in the beloved's affection, looks or fortune. 'Remover' is one who moves away, perhaps one who is unfaithful; 'bends ... to remove' means inclines to withdraw in turn. The word 'alters' returns in line 11 ('Love alters not'), so the poem answers its own definition.

title: O, no!
short: An emphatic, conversational negation, as if answering an objection: the voice of argument, not serene statement.
body: The exclamation breaks the poem's measured rhetoric with a spoken outburst. Vendler takes it as evidence that the poem is a rebuttal of another speaker's view; Booth notes its forceful, almost over-insistent tone. Some critics (following this line of argument) find the poem's very emphasis a sign of anxiety: the speaker protests that love cannot change precisely because he fears that it does.

title: an ever-fixed mark
short: A sea-mark: a beacon or landmark that guides ships and stays unmoved by storms.
body: A 'mark' (or sea-mark) was a conspicuous fixed object, such as a beacon, tower or lighthouse, used by sailors to steer (OED 'mark' n.1; 'sea-mark'). Shakespeare uses 'sea-mark' in Coriolanus 5.3 and Othello 5.2. Love 'looks on tempests and is never shaken': it observes storms without being moved, unlike the 'bark' of line 7. The image begins the nautical sequence of the second quatrain.

title: the star to every wandering bark
short: The Pole Star, by which lost ships (barks) navigate.
body: The 'star' is usually taken to be the Pole Star (Polaris), which stays almost fixed above the north pole and was the navigator's chief guide. A 'bark' is a small sailing ship. Love is the fixed point by which errant lovers ('wandering' ships) find their way. 'Wandering' anticipates the 'error' of line 13 (Latin errare, to wander), so that the couplet's word for a mistake recalls the lost ship. The star was a familiar Petrarchan image for the beloved as guide.

title: Whose worth's unknown, although his height be taken
short: The star's altitude can be measured for navigation, but its true value or nature remains unknown; so with love.
body: Sailors 'took the height' (measured the altitude) of the Pole Star with a quadrant or astrolabe to find their latitude. Its 'worth', however, cannot be known: the star's nature and its influence (in astrological thinking, its power over human lives) remain beyond calculation. The line says that love can be used and measured without being understood or fully valued. One commentary notes that 'taking the height' of something could also mean estimating its worth, which sharpens the contrast. 'His' here means 'its'.

title: Time's fool
short: Love is not the plaything or jester of Time; it is not made a fool of by ageing.
body: A 'fool' was a court jester kept for a master's amusement, or more generally a dupe, someone made sport of. Love is not Time's fool: Time cannot mock it or make it ridiculous by altering the lovers' looks. Shakespeare uses the phrase elsewhere, notably Hotspur's dying 'But thought's the slave of life, and life time's fool' (1 Henry IV 5.4). Personified Time carries his traditional sickle (l. 10).

title: his bending sickle's compass
short: Rosy youth falls within the curved sweep of Time's sickle, as grass falls to the reaper.
body: Time, like Death, was depicted as a reaper with a curved sickle or scythe. 'Compass' means range or reach, and also the arc swept by a curved blade (and the instrument that draws circles). Rosy lips and cheeks (youthful beauty) come within its reach and are cut down. The 'bending' sickle is answered by love, which does not bend (compare 'bends with the remover', l. 4). The quatrain concedes that beauty dies while insisting that love does not.

title: the edge of doom
short: To the very brink of Doomsday, the Last Judgement; love endures until the end of time.
body: 'Doom' means judgement, and 'the edge of doom' is the brink of Doomsday, the Last Judgement at the end of the world (compare Macbeth 4.1, 'the crack of doom'). 'Bears it out' means endures, holds out (like a ship riding out a storm, picking up the nautical images). Some read 'doom' more narrowly as death, so that love lasts until the lovers die; most editors prefer the apocalyptic sense, which matches the poem's absolute claims.

title: If this be error and upon me prov'd
short: A quasi-legal wager: if this is proved a mistake against me, then I never wrote and no man ever loved.
body: 'Error' means a mistake, but it also meant heresy (a wandering from true doctrine), and the Latin root errare recalls the 'wandering bark' of line 7. 'Upon me prov'd' is courtroom language: proved against me by evidence. Editors also note the legal term 'writ of error'. The couplet stakes everything on the definition, but its logic is circular: the existence of the poem itself is offered as proof that the speaker has 'writ'.

anchor: I never writ, nor no man ever lov'd
title: I never writ, nor no man ever lov'd
short: 'Writ' means 'wrote'; the double negative ('nor no man') was emphatic, not ungrammatical, in Elizabethan English.
body: 'Writ' was a normal past tense of 'write'. 'Nor no man' is an emphatic double negative, common in Shakespeare. The claim is a deliberate impossibility: the poet obviously has written, and men have loved, so the definition must stand. Critics differ on the tone. Some read a triumphant seal on the argument; others, noting that the couplet relies on a sophistical proof, sense defensiveness. The legal pun on 'writ' (a written legal document) continues the language of 'prov'd'.
